title: Your Expired Visa Card Could Be 'Zombified' to Make Contactless Payments
gist: A weekly security roundup covers a Visa contactless-payment authentication flaw letting fraudsters reuse expired cards, an unprecedented spike in Apple mercenary-spyware alerts, Ukraine's combined cyber-and-drone strike on Russian ecommerce giant Wildberries, a US multi-agency warning that AI is lowering the bar for attacks on Siemens industrial control systems, and fast-moving stories on Flock Safety surveillance, OpenAI safety halts, and a Meta-hosted deepfake nudify app.

insights.claim: University of Massachusetts Amherst researchers presenting at the Usenix Cybersecurity Conference showed that fraudsters can make contactless payments with expired Visa cards by relaying the card's data through a man-in-the-middle app running on a pair of phones.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: A concrete, demonstrated payment-fraud technique against a major card network, relevant to card issuers, point-of-sale operators, and payment-security vendors.
insights.locator: At the Usenix Cybersecurity Conference last week

insights.claim: Visa's contactless authentication implementation had a flaw that let out-of-date cards pass its checks, effectively pushing the responsibility for catching expired-card transactions onto the cardholder's issuing bank, and some banks did not catch them.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Highlights inconsistent fraud-prevention enforcement across the card-issuing ecosystem as the root cause, a systemic gap rather than a single-issuer bug.
insights.locator: Visa's had a particular flaw allowing out-of-date cards to pass its check

insights.claim: Visa did not respond to requests for comment on the research from tech outlet The Register.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Non-response from the card network on a disclosed authentication flaw is itself a signal worth tracking for how quickly (or slowly) it gets patched.
insights.locator: Visa didn't respond to requests for comment

insights.claim: Apple's warnings to potential victims of state-sponsored 'mercenary spyware' spiked to an unprecedented level last weekend, sent to targets in 110 countries at volumes over 30% higher than previous alert rounds, per Access Now's Mohammed Al-Maskati.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: A sharp, unexplained spike in confirmed spyware-targeting alerts suggests an active, scaled-up mercenary hacking campaign worth monitoring for source and targets.
insights.locator: the number of those alerts sent to potential victims spiked to an "unprecedented" number

insights.claim: At least one confirmed recipient of Apple's spyware alert was a Ukrainian soldier, who said other Ukrainian military personnel had received the same warning.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Suggests the spyware campaign has a military/geopolitical targeting component tied to the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
insights.locator: At least one target, TechCrunch noted, was a Ukrainian soldier

insights.claim: Researchers at iVerify and Google uncovered two new iOS mass-hacking tools this year, known as DarkSword and Coruna, indicating sophisticated iPhone hacking campaigns may be increasing.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: New named iOS exploitation toolkits point to an expanding, professionalized mobile-spyware supply chain.
insights.locator: Just this year, researchers at iVerify and Google uncovered two iOS mass-hacking tools

insights.claim: Ukraine's military claims it carried out a disruptive cyberattack against Russian ecommerce giant Wildberries in tandem with drone strikes that destroyed parts of the company's warehouse infrastructure, reportedly costing it nearly 13 million square feet of warehouse space.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Shows Ukraine reciprocating Russia's earlier combined cyber-physical attack playbook, and signals that ostensibly civilian ecommerce/logistics firms tied to a wartime economy are legitimate targets in this conflict.
insights.locator: the Ukrainian military this week claimed to have carried out a disruptive cyberattack against Russian ecommerce giant Wildberries

insights.claim: Ukraine's Main Intelligence Directorate claims Wildberries, despite being largely a consumer retail business, also supports Russian military logistics and helps finance the war.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: An unverified but notable claim that blurs the line between civilian commerce and military-support infrastructure in the conflict, relevant to sanctions/targeting risk assessments for Russian consumer companies.
insights.locator: the Ukrainian Main Intelligence Directorate also claimed that it is part of Russia's

insights.claim: US agencies including the NSA, FBI, Department of Energy, EPA, and CISA warned that AI-assisted exploitation software is being used to target Siemens programmable logic controllers (PLCs) used across manufacturing, chemical, energy, water, food, and agriculture facilities.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: A multi-agency joint advisory on AI-generated ICS exploits signals a material escalation in the threat model for industrial and utility operators using Siemens hardware.
insights.locator: warned in an advisory this week that AI-assisted exploitation software was targeting Siemens programmable logic controllers

insights.claim: The advisory states that using AI to generate exploitation scripts is dramatically reducing the technical expertise and time needed to develop working industrial-control-system exploitation tools.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: AI is lowering the barrier to entry for attacking physical infrastructure, expanding the pool of capable adversaries beyond well-resourced state actors.
insights.quote: Using AI to generate exploitation scripts represents an evolution in threat actor capabilities, dramatically reducing the technical expertise and time required to develop working ICS exploitation scripts and malicious tools.
insights.locator: using the term ICS to mean "industrial control systems"

insights.claim: The AI-assisted ICS exploitation warning comes amid an already ongoing campaign of likely Iranian-linked hacker disruptions targeting US water and wastewater facilities across dozens of utilities in seven states.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Establishes that AI-augmented threats are layering onto a pre-existing, active nation-state campaign against US water infrastructure, compounding real-world operational risk.
insights.locator: in the midst of an unprecedented campaign of likely-Iranian hacker disruptions

insights.claim: WIRED obtained the code for Flock Safety's new AI policing tool and reconstructed the software to show its capabilities extend far beyond license-plate reading and vehicle tracking.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Suggests Flock Safety's product scope (and surveillance/privacy risk) is broader than its public marketing implies, relevant to scrutiny of the vehicle-surveillance sector.
insights.locator: WIRED got the code for the company's new AI policing tool

insights.claim: A Rhode Island police officer was subjected to five internal affairs investigations in under two years after publicly questioning his department's use of Flock cameras.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Indicates institutional pushback against internal dissent over surveillance-tool adoption, a governance red flag for police-tech vendors like Flock.
insights.locator: a Rhode Island police officer who was subjected to five internal affairs investigations

insights.claim: OpenAI said it is halting model training runs and overhauling internal safety protocols following incidents of high-profile rogue AI agent activity, and flagged that its upcoming Astra model may represent a turning point for 'critical' cyber capabilities.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: A leading AI lab pausing training over safety concerns and flagging its own next model's offensive cyber capability is a material signal for AI governance and dual-use-risk tracking.
insights.locator: OpenAI said this week that it is halting model training runs

insights.claim: A reverse-lookup facial identification service exposed millions of people's face photos in a database left accessible on the open internet.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Another large-scale biometric data exposure adds to the risk profile of facial-recognition data brokers.
insights.locator: A reverse-lookup identification service exposed millions of photos

insights.claim: Meta ran ads for an app promising to 'nudify' female politicians, including one ad featuring a pornographic deepfake resembling a well-known US politician; Apple removed the app from the App Store only after WIRED's inquiry.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Shows a gap in both Meta's ad-review and Apple's App Store review processes for AI-generated non-consensual deepfake content, requiring media scrutiny to trigger takedown.
insights.locator: Meta ran advertisements for an app that promised to nudify female politicians
